newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ASML chief positive about chip future.
newsitem.headline: ASML chief positive about chip future.

text.p: ASM Lithography NV is confident semiconductor sales are set to double by 2000 and that demand for its chip-making machines will keep pace, its chairman said on Monday

"We are very positive about the future. We are in a market which is growing - doubling in three or four years time - we are on top of the technology, and it's not only we who think that, our customers also think so," said Willem Maris in an interview.
He said that although current patterns in the market for the "wafer steppers" made by ASML were not that positive, sales were set to pick up in the second half of the year or in early 1998.
"Timing is important -- and nobody knows when it's going to happen -- but that the market will increase is something that will happen," he said.
"1997 has been forecast as a year which feels the impact of the lower integrated circuit sales of 1996...because (wafer stepper) sales lag by six to nine months," said Maris.
Maris said the company was on course to finish 1997 with more market share than the current 19 percent, third behind market leader Nikon, with an estimated 45 percent, and Canon with 26 percent.
However, industry watchers say actual numbers of wafer stepper machines sold during 1997 are set to fall to between 900 and 1,000 compared with the 1,300 sold industry-wide last year.

Included in this year's total will be new-generation Deep Ultra Violet (DUV) steppers which can make smaller chips, cramming more onto a single wafer, thus boosting efficiency and cutting costs for customers.
"The costs of the products made with our machines are falling, that's one of the reasons for our success," he said.

Of the 205 machines sold by ASML in 1996 only eight were DUV. But Maris said demand levels for the new technology were such that 35-40 percent of sales in 1997 would be DUV machines, although he stopped short of predicting actual sales this year.
DUV machines were proving appealing to potential customers as sales of the older "I-Line" technology cooled off, said Maris.

"We are supporting the integrated circuit manufacturers in reducing costs. What we are claiming is that with an ASML stepper you have the cheapest wafers you can manufacture. That's one of the reasons we're gaining market share."

He said that the rapid changes in technology meant that the life span of wafer steppers was shortening. "Even when there are enough I-Lines in the market you need DUV and after that a new technology," he said.

ASML had technology projects in hand going out as far as 2010. The company in January reported a 66 percent rise in 1996 net profit to 218 million guilders ($114.5 million) on sales of 1.33 billion guilders, up from 917 million the year earlier.
Asked whether a doubling in sales would bring a doubling in profit by the year 2000 Maris replied: "I don't see a reason for profits to go down.

"The question is will profit double with doubling sales and my point is why not? You have only a few suppliers and every three years you have new products because technology changes so quickly. You can't make new technology without a new stepper. You have a technology race," he said.

"I expect our market share at the end of this year to be above 19 percent, and I have good reason to expect that because there will be new customers there...we don't expect to lose customers and as a consequence we ought to make market share," he said, reiterating a strategic aim of one third of the market. ($ = 1.904 Dutch Guilders)
